name: Automated Privilege Logging
title: Automated Privilege Logging
answer: Automated privilege logging is the use of software to identify documents and communications that are likely protected by attorney-client privilege or work product doctrine, then generate a privilege log describing the basis for withholding each item. In e-discovery, this replaces or augments manual review of large document sets where lawyers would otherwise read each file and record its author, recipient, date, and privilege rationale. The output is a structured list that can be produced to opposing counsel or a court, and the automation focuses on classification and metadata extraction rather than final legal judgment.

sections.body: Automated privilege logging is the use of software to identify documents and communications that are likely protected by attorney-client privilege or work product doctrine, then generate a privilege log describing the basis for withholding each item. In e-discovery, this replaces or augments manual review of large document sets where lawyers would otherwise read each file and record its author, recipient, date, and privilege rationale. The output is a structured list that can be produced to opposing counsel or a court, and the automation focuses on classification and metadata extraction rather than final legal judgment.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work typically runs on document review platforms that already store native files, email, and extracted text, often in cloud or on-premises environments used for litigation support. Privilege logging tools rely on indexed text, metadata fields, and sometimes pre-trained language models, but they do not require specialized hardware beyond what a standard e-discovery database already provides. Integration is usually through an application programming interface or a built-in module within the review workspace, so results stay inside the existing matter file.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The software first separates potentially privileged material from ordinary responsive documents using rules, keyword patterns, sender and recipient domains, and learned classifiers trained on prior privilege determinations. It then extracts the fields needed for a log, such as date, author, recipients, file name, and a short description, and proposes a privilege type like legal advice or trial preparation. A human reviewer confirms or corrects each entry, and the system records that decision to improve later suggestions. The method is supervised classification plus metadata extraction, not autonomous withholding.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risk is that an automated system may miss a privileged document and cause waiver, or over-designate non-privileged material and slow production. Courts generally require that a privilege log be accurate and that a lawyer has exercised reasonable care, so the human review step remains a professional obligation rather than a technical feature. Provenance matters because the log must trace each entry to the underlying document and the reviewer who approved it, and any model training data or prior decisions should be preserved for possible challenge. This page is not legal advice, and practices vary by jurisdiction.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Automated privilege logging is moving toward tighter integration with continuous active learning, where the same review workflow that ranks responsiveness also ranks privilege in one pass. Future systems may draft narrative privilege descriptions from the document text and link entries directly to the applicable ethical rule or case law citation. As courts see more disputes over machine-assisted logs, the field will likely develop clearer standards for sampling, validation, and disclosure of the tools used.
